name: Aisha Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the early loader shift at a large mine, checking tyres and fluid levels before the trucks start lining up. I'm still junior, so I ask the lead operator when I can't judge a tight turn, and I like getting a clean load into a truck. At 58 I can do the work, but the long climb down from the cab makes my knees complain after a wet day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the grand claims have settled down and we still need someone who can hear a loader cough before it quits. I'd also say the mine will keep trying small software changes because every minute of a stopped truck costs money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even an ordinary year doesn't feel entirely safe to me. I'm 58 and still on the junior roster; three months of household bills in the bank is useful, but a long break between mines would eat it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking my loader shifts and ask the lead operator to check my reversing and radio calls twice a month. If the hours hold through the first year, I'll put a little from each pay packet into the repair fund for our house instead of taking on a new car payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady around the machines, and less steady when the shift list goes up. The saving gives my partner and me room for one bad month, not a new life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a normal expense that makes that shift list matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our roof has a leak above the back room, and the roofer's estimate is sitting by the kettle. My grown daughter pays her own rent, so I can't pretend we're still paying school bills, but the house still asks for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep saving and also repair the roof. Which comes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The leak comes first if it gets worse. Otherwise I can set aside a small amount each payday, though I won't claim I know the exact repair bill yet.

say: I would say the **loader** still needs a careful operator when its engine sounds wrong.
I would tell my crew that small **software changes** will continue at the mine.
think: I worry that a **junior roster** leaves me vulnerable even in an ordinary year.
My **three months** of savings would shrink during a long gap between mines.
do: Keep taking **loader shifts** through the first year.
Ask the **lead operator** to check reversing and radio calls twice monthly.
Set aside pay for the **roof repair** when hours hold.
feel: Steady at the **machine**, uneasy when the shift list goes up.
S0.quote: I'm 58 and still on the junior roster; three months of household bills in the bank is useful, but a long break between mines would eat it.
fieldNote: She places her **ordinary risk** in the roster and house repairs rather than in a dramatic technology story.
Her plan assumes paid shifts continue, and she has no clear estimate yet for the **roof repair**.

steps.text: Keep taking loader shifts through the first year
Set aside pay from steady shifts for the roof repair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At lunch I'd say the office can use its clever programs, but a loader still needs a driver for now. I wouldn't sneer at the dispatch clerk if software takes over schedules; the dispatch clerk has bills the same as us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think mine management could use better scheduling to squeeze our breaks before any robot drives a machine. I'm still learning this loader, and I wouldn't win an argument that I'm the one operator they must keep if shifts are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the dispatch clerk to show me the new shift app rather than guessing from a printout. I'll keep my loader hours, and if a vacancy comes up at the neighbouring quarry I'll ask what licence they require before paying for any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy enough to listen carefully, but I can still picture myself going to work tomorrow. Seeing the clerk lose hours would make the change real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the clerk when you see her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mara, our dispatch clerk, whether the app lets us flag a road closure before a truck gets sent down it. She knows which instructions from the screen can make a mess on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply at the quarry immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask about its licence first and stay on my current shift if it holds. I don't have spare money to buy a certificate for a vacancy that might never open.

say: I would say the **loader** still needs a driver during slower robot adoption.
I would stand up for the **dispatch clerk** if software cuts her hours.
think: I suspect tighter **scheduling** could reduce breaks before robots arrive.
My **junior position** makes me replaceable if management trims shifts.
do: Ask the **dispatch clerk** how to use the shift app.
Continue **loader shifts** while paid hours hold.
Check the neighbouring **quarry licence** before paying for training.
feel: Uneasy about **hours**, especially after seeing a colleague affected.
S1.quote: I wouldn't sneer at the dispatch clerk if software takes over schedules; the dispatch clerk has bills the same as us.
fieldNote: She expects the earliest effect through **schedules** and co-workers rather than immediate replacement at the controls.
Her interest in quarry work is **conditional** on a real vacancy and licence requirement; she has not applied.

steps.text: Ask the dispatch clerk to show the new shift app
Keep working paid loader shifts while hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew two years is no time at all, even if the machines cannot drive themselves until around 2031. The planners and dispatch team would feel the thinking AI in 2028, and I would want the mine to tell us plainly what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 my own cab work may still exist, but I can't build retirement on three extra years of driving. At 60 I'd be competing for fewer shifts, and at 63, when robots arrive, I'd have to expect my loader hours could disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'll ask the training office whether they will fund the plant-maintenance certificate; I will enroll if they pay the fee and keep me on shifts. In the first year after 2028 I'll continue driving while the loader is staffed, and I'll reduce our house spending so we have cash by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed when I count those years on my fingers. I can do the next shift, but I wake up wondering whether the house and the work will run out together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would postpone replacing the kitchen cupboards and keep the old car. I wouldn't cut the roof repair; water coming in costs more if you ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown son I may need advice about vacancies, not money from him. He has his own household, and I don't want to make our retirement his bill.

say: I would tell the crew that **2028** puts dispatch and planning at risk first.
I would ask the mine for a plain account of **robot plans** for 2031.
think: I expect my **loader hours** could vanish when robots arrive around 2031.
At **63**, competing for reduced shifts would make retirement uncertain.
do: Ask whether the mine will **fund maintenance training** while preserving shifts.
Keep driving the **loader** after 2028 while staffed.
Postpone **kitchen cupboards** and keep the old car.
feel: Alarmed by the **short runway** to possible lost income.
S2.quote: I can't build retirement on three extra years of driving.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 office impact** from possible loss of her own operating hours around 2031.
Her maintenance course depends on **funding and shifts**; spending cuts begin while she seeks that answer.

steps.text: Enroll in plant-maintenance training if the mine funds it and preserves shifts
Keep driving the loader after 2028 while it remains staffed
Postpone kitchen cupboards and keep the old car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years lets the mine give people a proper warning before the office changes in 2031. I would still ask what happens to loader drivers when capable robots arrive around 2034, because a warning without work is thin comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when the thinking systems arrive and 66 when robots can do the driving. I might get close to leaving full shifts by then, but I haven't been promised a pension amount that lets us live on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll sit down with my partner and write our actual monthly bills beside the savings balance. I'll stay on the loader, ask for the maintenance course if the mine funds it, and after 2031 I'll check the roster every month before deciding whether to apply at the quarry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, but I can breathe with five years in front of me. The part that bothers me is promising my partner a retirement date I cannot yet pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What number would change your choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If six months of expenses were sitting there untouched, I could take a short training break. We have about three months now, so I need wages alongside any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait on the quarry application?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would apply if our loader shifts actually fall or a suitable vacancy is posted. The quarry is near enough to drive to, but leaving a paying shift for a rumour would be foolish.

say: I would ask for **clear warning** before office work changes in 2031.
I would ask how the mine plans to employ **loader drivers** after 2034.
think: I may be **66** when capable robots arrive, but retirement income is unconfirmed.
I cannot promise my partner a **retirement date** without checking our bills.
do: Write down **monthly bills** with my partner this year.
Stay on **loader shifts** while they remain available.
Apply at the **quarry** if shifts fall and a suitable vacancy appears.
feel: Worried yet able to **breathe** with several years to plan.
S3.quote: The part that bothers me is promising my partner a retirement date I cannot yet pay for.
fieldNote: She resists treating age as automatic **retirement security**, since she has no confirmed income figure.
Her quarry application is tied to **falling shifts** and a real vacancy, not merely the 2031 announcement.

steps.text: Keep taking loader shifts while the mine offers them
Apply at the neighbouring quarry if shifts fall and a suitable vacancy opens
Enroll in mine-funded maintenance training if wages continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time for the mine to train people honestly if it chooses. By 2036 the office may run on thinking AI, and by around 2039 the loaders may run without us; those are two different dates for our crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 68 in 2036 and 71 when the robots arrive. I hope to be off full shifts by then, but the roof and everyday bills may force me to keep earning longer than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working and put a fixed small sum from each regular pay into a separate savings account this year. I'll ask the mine for a written estimate of any retirement benefit, then revisit paid work each year; if my health and money allow it, I'll reduce shifts before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one feels less urgent, though not easy. Ten years lets me ask hard questions while I can still climb into a cab without thinking twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you reduce shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The numbers would need to cover our bills and the roof, and my back would need to tell me it is time. I'd rather work fewer shifts by choice than be sent home by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a longer warning change what you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children we're checking the figures, not announcing a retirement party. They deserve to know what we're doing, but they have their own lives to pay for.

say: I would say **2036 and 2039** create different deadlines for office staff and loader crews.
I would press the mine to offer **honest training** during the decade.
think: At **71**, I hope to have left full shifts before robots take loader work.
The **roof and bills** may require me to keep earning longer.
do: Continue **paid loader work** while health and shifts permit.
Put a **fixed sum** from regular pay into separate savings.
Ask for a written **retirement estimate** before reducing shifts.
feel: Less urgent, but aware that **money and health** still decide.
S4.quote: I'd rather work fewer shifts by choice than be sent home by a machine.
fieldNote: The longer timetable overlaps with the years when **health** may constrain physical work even without robots.
She wants to reduce shifts by choice, yet makes that **conditional** on verified income and house costs.

steps.text: Continue paid loader work while health and shifts permit
Transfer a fixed sum from regular pay into separate savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I get only until about 2031 before a robot could do my driving, and I can't assume my savings will last. Paid maintenance training while I still have shifts would help, and so would a clear timetable from the mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I actually want to stop. I like the machine and the people, and I'd keep some paid shifts if my knees and the mine let me.

headlineQuote: I like the machine and the people, and I'd keep some paid shifts if my knees and the mine let me.
portrait: Aisha is a **58-year-old junior** loader operator with secondary school education and about three months of household expenses saved.
She likes the **machine work**, but worries that a weak roster and roof repairs could drain her cushion.
She expects **thinking AI** to change dispatch first and capable robots to threaten her own shifts three years later.
She seeks **paid training** and verified retirement figures before making a costly move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her too little time to replace loader income before robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Mine-funded maintenance training** with continued shifts and a clear robot timetable would help her plan.
